OUTLINE VIEW

Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review mechanisms of action and toxicities of chemotherapeutic agents frequently used in the
management of bone sarcomas.
Describe the chemotherapy regimens used for the management of osteosarcoma and Ewing
sarcoma.
Assess the potential role for systemic management of other histologies.
Examine unique considerations for the orthopaedic oncologist with regard to systemic
management.
Chemotherapeutic Agents for Bone Sarcoma
A basic knowledge of the mechanisms of action and toxicities of chemotherapeutic agents is
important for sarcoma surgeons.

Classic toxicities include renal tubular injury (methotrexate), cardiac toxicity (doxorubicin),
neurotoxicity/neuropathy (cisplatin and vincristine), ototoxicity and renal toxicity (cisplatin),
and hemorrhagic cystitis (cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide).
In anticipation of chemotherapy, the diagnostic workup for a child or young adult with
osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma should include laboratory studies (complete blood count,
complete metabolic panel, glomerular filtration rate), audiology testing, echocardiography, and
fertility counseling. Long-term toxicity monitoring is conducted through survivors’ clinics.

Chemotherapeutic Agents for Bone Sarcoma
Cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents, as used in the systemic management of bone
sarcomas, act by inhibiting the cell cycle and/or by inducing apoptosis of rapidly dividing
cells. A basic knowledge of the mechanisms of action, toxicities, and adverse effects of
frequently used agents is important for sarcoma surgeons.
The systemic management of osteosarcoma typically includes methotrexate,
doxorubicin, and cisplatin (MAP). Methotrexate is an anti-metabolite (specifically, an anti-
folate agent). Adverse effects may include myelosuppression and renal tubular injury,
the risks of which are mitigated by the co-administration of leucovorin and urinary
alkalinization, respectively. Reduction in bone density is a late toxicity. Doxorubicin is an
anthracycline, which intercalates with DNA and inhibits replication. Cardiac toxicity is a
primary concern, including the potential for acute cardiomyopathy or late
cardiomyopathy, congestive heart failure, or arrhythmia. Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator
co-administered to diminish free radical formation, limits cardiac muscle damage.
Cisplatin is a platinum-containing, alkylating-like agent, which may cause renal
dysfunction, ototoxicity, and neuropathy.1-4
The systemic management of Ewing sarcoma typically includes vincristine, doxorubicin,
and cyclophosphamide (VDC)/ifosfamide and etoposide (IE). Vincristine is a vinca
alkaloid, disrupting the cell cycle by blocking microtubule polymerization.
Neurotoxicity/neuropathy is a common adverse effect. Cyclophosphamide and
ifosfamide are alkylating agents. Hemorrhagic cystitis is a classic toxicity, particularly in
patients undergoing concurrent pelvic radiation therapy; however, this risk is mitigated

via co-administration of mesna. Etoposide creates DNA strand breaks by inhibiting
topoisomerase. Leukopenia is an important adverse effect.1-4
In addition to these agent-specific toxicities, adverse effects common to many (if not all)
of these chemotherapeutic agents include myelosuppression, gastrointestinal
symptoms, and alopecia. Long-term toxicities observed after exposure to multiple
agents include secondary malignancy (typically acute myeloid leukemia) in children
treated with the use of doxorubicin, cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, or
etoposide and delayed or arrested puberty and infertility in children treated with the use
of cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, or ifosfamide.1-4
Given these adverse effects and toxicities, children or young adults with a newly
diagnosed bone sarcoma should undergo laboratory studies, including a complete blood
count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and quantification of glomerular filtration rate;
audiology testing; echocardiography; and consideration of referral to a fertility clinic.
Similarly, long-term follow-up involves not only sarcoma surveillance but also monitoring
for late toxicity through a survivor’s clinic.1
Systemic Management of Osteosarcoma
High-grade, conventional osteosarcoma in children and young adults is managed with the use
of MAP.
Management typically involves two cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection,
and four cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy.
Tumor necrosis greater than 90% after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is an important favorable
prognostic factor.

Systemic Management of Osteosarcoma
High-grade, conventional osteosarcoma in children and young adults typically is
managed via surgical resection and MAP chemotherapy.

Most patients with osteosarcoma have micro-metastatic disease, even if only a single
site of disease is visible on staging imaging studies; this explains the high mortality rate
(approximately 80%) in the pre-chemotherapy era.3,5,6 Neoadjuvant/adjuvant
chemotherapy was introduced in the 1970s, initially as a stop-gap treatment option
while patients and surgeons awaited the custom fabrication of surgical implants.7 Two
seminal, randomized controlled trials in the late 1980s demonstrated a 2-year disease-
free survival ranging from 55% to 66% in patients with localized disease managed via
chemotherapy.8,9 These early trial regimens included MAP, bleomycin,
cyclophosphamide, and actinomycin D.
Currently, most centers use MAP chemotherapy as a first-line osteosarcoma treatment
option (Figure 1); MAP chemotherapy is delivered as two cycles of neoadjuvant
management (approximately 10 weeks), followed by surgical resections, and
subsequently four cycles of adjuvant management (approximately 20 weeks).4 Although
the need for custom surgical implants currently is far less common than it was in the
past, the potential advantages of preoperative chemotherapy include immediate
management of any subclinical (or gross) metastatic disease; possible reduction in tumor
size (less common in osteosarcoma) and improved patient candidacy for limb salvage;
and, most importantly, assessment of chemotherapy response as measured by tumor
necrosis in the resection specimen.3

Good histologic response, typically defined as greater than 90% necrosis, is a key
positive prognostic factor. Although current management achieves an all-comers 5-year
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:45 AM
AAOS | Systemic Management of Bone Sarcomas
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004041
5/16

overall survival rate ranging from 60% to 70% in patients with localized disease, good
histologic response may be associated with a 5-year overall survival rate of 80%.10-12
Upfront surgical management with postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy may be
considered in certain clinical contexts (eg, if a diagnosis of high-grade, conventional
osteosarcoma cannot be definitively made on initial biopsy). No difference in outcome
has been observed between patients treated via this approach and patients receiving
neoadjuvant systemic therapy.13 In addition, a recent clinical trial demonstrated no
improvement after postoperative regimen intensification with the use of IE in patients
with localized disease but poor histologic response; however, this regimen continues to
be used in patients with metastatic disease.14
Although most patients present with micro-metastatic disease, patients who present
with evidence of overt metastases on imaging studies have a notably poorer prognoses.
First-line systemic treatment of patients with metastatic disease is the same as that of
patients with primary disease; however, surgical resection of lung metastases
(metastasectomy), if feasible, is associated with improved prognosis. Five-year overall
survival among patients with metastatic disease ranges from 20% to 30% but may be as
high as 40% in patients with a limited number of respectable nodules and likely is less
than 5% in patients with unresectable pulmonary (or other visceral or bony)
metastases.15-17 Although no single established second-line therapy exists for relapsed
disease, potential regimens include high-dose ifosfamide; cyclophosphamide and
etoposide; gemcitabine and docetaxel; and, more recently, kinase inhibitors, such as
sorafenib and regorafenib.5
The management of high-grade, intramedullary non-osteoblastic histologic subtypes,
including chondroblastic, fibroblastic, and telangiectatic subtypes, is analogous to that of
conventional osteosarcoma.4,5 Notably, tumor necrosis in response to preoperative
chemotherapy is higher in fibroblastic and telangiectatic subtypes, and lower in
chondroblastic subtypes compared with conventional osteoblastic tumors. For all high-
grade, intramedullary subtypes, with the exception of chondroblastic subtypes, tumor
necrosis is prognostic of oncologic outcomes.11 Parosteal osteosarcoma typically is a
low-grade, surface-based tumor, and low-grade osteosarcomas do not require systemic
therapy. An important differential diagnosis is periosteal osteosarcoma, which also is a

surface-based lesion but of intermediate to high grade.18 The role of systemic
management for periosteal osteosarcoma is controversial.19,20
Systemic Management of Ewing Sarcoma
Ewing sarcoma is managed with the use of VDC/IE.
Management typically involves six cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection, and
eight cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy.
Tumor necrosis greater than 90% after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is an important positive
prognostic factor.

Systemic Management of Ewing Sarcoma
Nonmetastatic Ewing sarcoma typically is managed via a combination of local control
(surgery and/or radiation therapy) and a systemic regimen (Figure 2), including VDC/IE.
This usually is administered as six cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (approximately
12 to 14 weeks), followed by surgical management or definitive radiation therapy, and
then eight additional cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy.4

Key advancements in the evolution of the systemic management of Ewing sarcoma have
included the adoption of high-dose21 and intensified (every 2 weeks) cycle22 regimens
and the addition of IE (beneficial in localized but not metastatic disease).23 Current
treatment regimens in combination with surgical resection allow for 5-year overall
survival rates ranging from 70% to 80%.22,23 Similar to osteosarcoma, complete (100%)
or near complete (>90%) tumor necrosis is associated with improved outcomes.24,25
First-line systemic therapy typically is the same for patients presenting with metastatic
disease. Notably, the use of IE in addition to VDC may not be beneficial in patients with
metastatic disease;23,26,27 regardless, the VDC/IE regimen typically is used.28 Similar to
osteosarcoma, limited or surgically resectable pulmonary disease is associated with a
relatively improved prognosis; however, whole-lung radiation therapy also may be
used.29,30 Potential second- or third-line regimens for relapsed disease include
irinotecan and temozolamide, gemcitabine and docetaxel, or cabozantinib.28
Doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide may be associated with a
long-term risk of secondary myelodysplasia/acute myeloid leukemia; this is a particular
concern in children and young adults treated via the current VDC/IE regimen, with a
cumulative 5-year incidence rate as high as 11%.31
Systemic Management of Other Histologies
Secondary bone sarcomas associated with Paget disease and radiation therapy are managed
in a fashion similar to that of conventional osteosarcoma.
Localized conventional chondrosarcoma typically is not managed via with chemotherapy;
however, dedifferentiated and mesenchymal chondrosarcoma are indications for systemic
therapy.

Systemic Management of Other Histologies
Although conventional osteosarcoma typically arises in children and young adults, a
second epidemiologic peak occurs in elderly patients, presenting at a mean age of 75 to

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004041
9/16

79 years. Osteosarcoma in these patients usually occurs secondary to Paget disease of
bone or prior radiation therapy and is associated with considerably poorer 5-year
survival rates (<40%) compared with pediatric disease.32 Systemic management of
osteosarcoma in patients older than 40 years, including those with secondary sarcomas,
often involves doxorubicin and cisplatin because of poor tolerance of methotrexate.5
Conventional chondrosarcomas are considered chemoresistant, and management of
localized disease typically consists of surgical resection alone; however, systemic
management does have a role in the management of two histologic subtypes of
chondrosarcoma: dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma and mesenchymal
chondrosarcoma.
Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is an extremely aggressive tumor, most commonly
arising in patients in their fifties to seventies, and is characterized by a high-grade,
noncartilaginous component arising within a lower-grade cartilage background.33 The
dedifferentiated component may have the appearance of an osteoblastic, fibrous, or
anaplastic spindle cell sarcoma. Osteosarcoma-style chemotherapy typically is used
(often with omission of methotrexate in older patients); however, benefit is modest, with
5-year overall survival rates ranging from 5% to 35%.4,33,34 Mesenchymal
chondrosarcoma is a rare tumor that can arise in bone or soft tissues, with a reported
median patient age of 30 years.35 Chemotherapy, often using Ewing sarcoma protocols,
has been shown to improve patient outcomes;35,36 however, randomized trial data are
lacking.
Special Considerations for Orthopaedic Oncologists
Adjuvant chemotherapy typically is resumed 2 to 3 weeks after definitive surgical resection;18
delayed chemotherapy resumption may negatively affect patient outcomes.
In patients with a pathologic fracture, neoadjuvant chemotherapy can be completed as
planned or upfront surgical resection can be performed.

Special Considerations for Orthopaedic Oncologists
Minimizing surgical complications to allow for early resumption of adjuvant
chemotherapy is critical for sarcoma surgeons and should be considered in formulating
the surgical plan. Systemic management typically is resumed 2 to 3 weeks
postoperatively; delayed chemotherapy resumption of more than 3 to 4 weeks is
associated with poor oncologic outcomes.37,38
Pathologic fracture through bone sarcoma is associated with increased mortality (5-year
event free survival rate, 49% versus 67%) but is not thought to be an absolute
contraindication to subsequent limb salvage.39 Completion of neoadjuvant
chemotherapy despite pathologic fracture may in facilitate limb salvage candidacy, and
pathologic fractures can be expected to heal during systemic management.39,40 If
margin-negative surgical management is deemed technically feasible at the time of
fracture, upfront resection also is reasonable.41
